judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is sweeping — 'all confidential information or trade secrets ... including, but not limited to' client names and 'all records and other documents made and/or maintained in connection with Wells Fargo Advisors business' — so the outer boundary of the catch-all is uncertain, particularly whether publicly available client identities are covered. That is a genuine general-versus-specific problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 11(b) then calls the same material 'Confidential Records or Documents', a label never defined here, and Paragraph 12(a) restricts solicitation of clients the employee merely 'learned of', so the three provisions overlap imprecisely. judgments.reasoning_cat1: The surrender obligation attaches to 'any Confidential Records or Documents', a term that does not match the defined 'Confidential Information and Documents' in 11(a) — a mechanical slip that changes what must be returned. judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against 11(a)'s definition and Paragraph 15's survival language, the mismatched label is the only friction; the substantive duties are otherwise consistent. A court would likely harmonise them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any Wells Fargo Advisors client that you had contact with or otherwise learned of' is very broad and 'otherwise learned of' has no discernible boundary; 'solicit or cause or permit to be solicited' adds a permissive-conduct standard hard to apply. judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with Paragraph 11's confidentiality duties and Paragraph 14(c)'s injunctive carve-out without contradiction, though Paragraph 10(b)(ii)(A) creates a separate, differently defined competition disincentive. No square conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds Paragraph 13(c)'s adjustment mechanism and Paragraph 9(a)'s final-compensation calculation, all consistent with each other and with the at-will provision. No conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disclosures describe a far wider arbitration promise than the operative clause — arbitrating with 'a client, or any other person' — and contain the garbled 'the arbitration forum in the claim is filed' and a parenthetical that lumps NLRA claims into 'State unemployment insurance'. judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction to enforce Paragraphs 11 and 12. Its one-sidedness (only Wells Fargo may go to court) could invite a construe-against-the-drafter argument, but the words themselves are clear.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against Paragraph 8 ('this Agreement serves only as a synopsis' of other arrangements), Paragraph 6 (HR policies not superseded) and Paragraph 3 (the unattached, unilaterally amendable Compensation Plan), and against Paragraph 15's own, differently worded survival list.
